subject: frostAxe
pitch:
Category: Fantasy weapon.
Subject: frost-forged battle axe.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm planning a frost-forged battle axe prop in a League of Legends stylized aesthetic, with bold painterly shapes and glowing icy details. Since it's a static prop without articulation, I'll still add a single root joint at the origin so the builder has an anchor point for the parts.

For the design, I'm imagining the axe standing upright, planted butt-first into a small cluster of jagged ice crystals at floor level, with the haft rising vertically and the blade up top, around 1.7 m tall overall. I'll construct it using documented builder primitives like part, extrude, lathe, sweep, spike, and rod, paired with the paint/shading utilities like mix, noise, gradient, and countershade to get that icy, hand-painted look.

I'm orienting the axe so the blade sweeps forward along +Z in a crescent shape with a frost spike balancing the back, outlined in the extrude's x-y plane with thickness running along x, and sketching out the haft as a swept vertical path with dark wood grain shading.

For the frost-forged haft, I'm planning dark navy wood with silver bands rather than plain steel, using a swept rod with a thicker radius near the grip. Then I'm laying out the base components: an ice crystal cluster made of low-poly cones at the foot of the haft, nestled into a small icy mound built from a simple cylinder/lathe shape.

Working out exact dimensions now -- the icy base cylinder sits flush at y=0, with crystal spikes rising from its surface at tilted angles so their bases touch the mound naturally. I'm using angled spike geometry with hexagonal facets for a crystalline look, randomizing their placement and size around the ring for a scattered, natural cluster.

For color I'm mixing icy blues and whites, making a few of the inner crystals glow for an enchanted effect. Now I'm shifting to the haft design, planning the grip wrap using small torus shapes stacked along the handle to simulate leather binding rings over the dark wood shaft.

Actually, a spiral wrap would look more convincing than stacked rings, so I'm sweeping a thin leather strand along a spiral path up the grip, tuning the turns and pitch so it covers from y=0.3 to about 0.96 with enough segments to look smooth without being too dense.

Now I'm thinking about adding a metal collar and butt cap below the grip near the ice base, sketching a lathe profile with flared points to give it an ornate socket shape.

Then I'm planning the mid-haft langets—thin steel strips as narrow boxes positioned around the shaft near the head—and starting to lay out the axe head itself: a central socket mounted around y≈1.45 with a flared ornate cylinder shape and a frustum-like body for the head.

Now I'm sketching the blade outline in the YZ plane as a bearded-axe crescent shape, plotting coordinate points for the upper horn tip, lower horn, and curved cutting edge to get that classic convex blade profile extending outward from the haft.

Since a hole can't work in a single extruded outline, I'll layer the glowing ice crescent as a separate piece on top of the face instead. Now I'm plotting the outline points clockwise from the haft, defining the spine curve and sharp upper tip coordinates.

I'm continuing to map out the lower tip and edge points, making the lower tip slightly shorter for asymmetry, and reconsidering the C-D edge shape -- thinking through whether the notch should curve inward or bulge outward to get that proper crescent, horn-like bearded-axe silhouette.

Rethinking scale: a full moon-shaped span of 1.1m is way oversized for a 1.6m haft, so I'm scaling the head down to roughly 0.7m tall with a half-height of 0.34, closer to an Olaf-style exaggerated but plausible battle axe. I'm defining the outline points with a concave crescent edge, marking certain tips as sharp while leaving others smoothed.

Still plotting coordinates...

Mirroring the upper spine symmetric to the lower one, I'm checking the polygon stays non-self-intersecting and verifying the blade's thinness at the midpoint cross-section around z=0.34.

The resulting shape forms a crescent bite with material filling where z is less than the edge curve, giving a puppet-like chunky cutting edge with a 0.03 thickness and 0.01 bevel—good enough, no need for an extra bright strip.

Writing paint shader logic...

Now I'm thinking about adding etched glowing runes to the blade faces using thin plane geometries positioned just off each face, textured with cyan glowing stroke patterns, while noting the mirrored text on the opposite side doesn't need to be readable.

Actually, the mirroring doesn't matter much since I'll keep the design symmetric enough for either side. I'll place the decorative plane at the head center with a small offset, sized half a unit, and map the drawing coordinates onto it to create a concentric crescent ornamental pattern.

Writing SVG mirroring and coordinate mapping...

Converting the inset crescent line coordinates to u/v units, following the offset edge points down through the tip and tracing a smooth curved path through them.

I'll place a snowflake centered where z=0.17, y=0, giving a radius of about 14 units, with six spokes and smaller branches drawn off each one.

Checking plane positions for the blade thickness: the faces sit at roughly ±0.024 offset from center, and I need to verify the snowflake spokes stay within the blade's actual shape boundaries rather than extending into transparent cutaway regions.

Now I'm designing the socket where the haft meets the axe head, plus a glowing crystal gem embedded at the head's base. I'm defining the socket as a lathed shape around the haft axis, roughly ±0.17 in height with flared collars, using a boxy hexagonal cylinder profile for the central section.

Shaping the back spike outline...

Still placing ice spikes...

Now I want icicles hanging downward from the lower blade edge at a couple positions, plus a glowing gem — maybe an elongated octahedron — positioned either on the blade face or on the socket's side faces.

I'm sizing the gem to sit at the socket sides, scaled non-uniformly so it reads clearly even from a distance, partially embedded into the socket radius. I'm also considering adding langets — metal mounting plates running from the socket down onto the haft for a more authentic weapon look.

Now I'm adding a draped cloth ribbon hanging below the socket, using a flattened catmull-rom sweep with varying elliptical radii to simulate a tattered blue frost pennant trailing down the haft.

Writing haft paint shader...

I'm checking that mix accepts ColorInput strings and paint returns valid output, renaming the unused normal param, and keeping colors under the flat-color limit since paints don't count toward it. Now I'm adding steel-colored torus bands along the haft at specific heights to represent decorative rings.

Now I'm designing the material palette: a cold steel paint blending blue-gray tones with noise and gradient, a darker steel for the head body with frost speckles, and a warm gold accent paint for trim bands and collars to contrast with the cold blue. I'm placing gold tori on the socket and haft, plus a gold pommel cap, then starting on the icy base mound geometry at the bottom.

Adding scattered low rocks around the base, then placing a ring of nine ice crystal spikes with randomized angles, lean directions, lengths, and radii, colored in icy blues and given a glow effect.

I'm selectively glowing the largest crystal, gems, and runes for contrast while leaving others matte, and considering adding a handful of small floating ice shards orbiting near the blade for visual flair, keeping the count modest so it doesn't look cluttered.

I'm also tuning overall height proportions—adjusting the haft, socket, and crystal lengths so the axe stays large but not oversized—and sketching a raised inner frost ridge panel on the blade face, working out inset coordinates that stay within the blade's edge boundary.

For the panel color, I'm leaning toward a dark navy flat tone so the glowing snowflake pops with better contrast, with walls painted gold and faces navy using a normal-based paint rule.

I also need to fix an overlap problem — the crescent accent lines near the blade edge are clipping into the panel at certain y-values, so I'm resizing the panel polygon smaller and recalculating the crescent line offsets so they stay a consistent gap from the edge all the way from the base to the tip.

Converting the remaining fin coordinates to pixel space and plotting them as a cyan polyline outline.

Now I'm positioning a snowflake decoration at the panel's center, calculating its radius so it fits within the panel bounds, then drawing it as six spokes radiating from the center with small branch lines partway along each spoke.

For the mirrored -X side, I need to flip the drawing orientation since "right" now corresponds to the opposite texture direction, so I'm wrapping the SVG in a transform that translates and scales by -1 to mirror it correctly. I'm also double-checking that the viewBox aspect ratio matches the physical plane dimensions and that stroke widths scale properly to pixels.

Now I'm verifying the plane's z-position relative to the blade center, confirming the texture's zero point lines up correctly with the geometry. I'm setting up the glass panel as a plane geometry with a texture map applied as emissive so the colors show through properly on the white base, but I'm noticing the panel sits too far off the blade surface — about 13mm floating gap — since the panel offset doesn't account for the blade's actual thickness at that point.

I'm deciding to split this into two separate planes with different textures, one for the snowflake pattern closer out, one for the crescent line closer to the blade surface, to avoid that floating gap, accepting a small 4mm offset as an acceptable compromise. Then I'm working through how the paint gradient on the blade body should look, with the frosting brighter near the cutting edge.

Adding frost crack texture...

Checking walls near the spine where s[0]<0.33 for gold edge treatment, with the frosty wall look at the cutting edge—extending this gold accent up toward the tip region too.

Setting up the imports and paint helpers for the build, then starting the metadata export and gold paint definition for the battle axe...

Still writing color definitions...

Now I'm setting up the build function, defining the root joint and key height constants for the axe, using a seeded random generator for consistent variation.

Adding snow-capped cylinder base and scattering small flattened rock pieces around it in a circular pattern with randomized rotations and scale.

For the crystal spikes, I'm looping to place ten tapered spike shapes radiating outward and upward from the base, randomizing their angle, length, radius, and lean direction, and assigning colors cyclically with hexagonal cross-sections.

I'm checking that crystals leaning outward won't collide with the haft since they're angled away from center, then designing the central haft as a tapered octagonal rod running from the base up to the top, deciding to use a simple fixed radius instead of a taper array for simplicity.

I'm adding a subtle swell to the haft by using a sweep with varying radii along its length to give it a slight organic bulge, then planning a spiral leather wrap around the haft using a helical path with multiple turns and a thin cross-section tube.

I'm also adding decorative gold torus rings at the top and bottom of the wrap to cap off the leather binding.

Then I'm planning four thin box-shaped strips (langets) positioned around the handle at offset angles, oriented alternately along the x and z axes to sit flush against the sides, spanning the handle height.

Positioning the strips so they partly tuck into the socket and overlap the gold ring, colored steel. Now I'm working out the lathe profile for the pommel cap, defining a closed polygon of coordinate points to shape its rounded contour.

Deciding to color the whole cap gold since it already has a gold ring, and confirming the haft bottom sits safely inside it. For the head, I'm setting the socket lathe at the hilt's top position with dark steel coloring and gold tori rings above and below, then adding a crystal spike capping the top with a glowing ice-blue hexagonal section, plus a ring of four smaller tilted crystals surrounding it.

Now I'm working out the blade outline typing issue — the array mixes plain coordinate pairs with sharp-corner markers, which TypeScript would infer incorrectly, so I need to either cast it or define an explicit union type for points before passing it to the extrude call with thickness, bevel, and color settings.

I'll keep smoothing at 0 for the blade to avoid risky corner-rounding near thin sharp tips, and add denser points for a cleaner edge. For the panel, I'm setting up a paint function that checks the normal's x-component to choose between navy and gold, then applying it with its own thickness and bevel values before moving on to extrude the rear fang.

I need to fix the fang outline so it starts flush with the socket boundary instead of overlapping it, then shape the tip further out with upward curvature. Rather than building a new paint for the fang, I'll just reuse the blade's paint function so the tip gets that same frosted-white gradient while the walls stay gold except near the tip. Now I'm working out placement for small spine crystals along the blade, picking coordinate pairs that trace a line up the spine.

I'm computing the exact positions, directions, and lengths for each spike and icicle along the blade's spine, interpolating y-values between known points to get bases that sit correctly above and below the centerline.

Now I'm adding floating crystal shards scattered near the bite area, using scaled octahedron geometry with slight random rotations and a soft glow to give them a loose, shattered look.

Then I'm placing embedded gems into the handle sockets on both sides, sizing and positioning them to overlap slightly with the carved socket so they look set into the blade, with a subtle glow for added richness. I'm also starting to sketch out a ribbon sweep beneath the socket using a smooth curve.

I'll color the ribbons blue-ish front and pale blue back. Skipping the hanging charm idea, I'll add a glow effect to the blade planes, and I'll leave shaft frost minimal since the crystal spikes already cover that visual.

I'm checking the gold tori dimensions on the socket to make sure they hug the haft properly, then writing a function to generate branching snowflake patterns as SVG path data for the rune texture.

For the crescent texture, I'm plotting a polyline with small dots at vertices, and building a texture helper that wraps SVG bodies with optional horizontal mirroring for applying patterns to both faces of a plane.

I'm offsetting the flake and crescent positions from the panel surface and working through how the mirrored coordinate system maps drawn elements back to actual Z positions for planes on the negative X side, verifying the math checks out to 0.56 - u/125.

Checking that plane normals point outward so textures render on front faces only, and confirming the depth offsets avoid z-fighting with the panel. I'm also considering small decorative touches like gold rivets or frost-forged ice spikes flanking the blade root, though I may skip some of these as optional embellishments.

I'm working through implementation details like random rotations for octahedron shards, flat shading for gems and rocks, and making sure the glow effect applies correctly across shared materials without breaking on textured plane parts. Defining the dark steel paint gradient...

Writing blade paint logic...

Checking that paint sheet density holds at a few millimeters and that mirror normal sign doesn't matter, then confirming the base cylinder sits flush at y=0 with everything else stacked above it.

Writing lathe outlines for socket and blade...

The tips stay thin enough near the wedge between spine and edge, and the gold wall near the socket only needs the spine. I'm sketching out the panel outline as a point array and setting up the spike helper function with base, direction, length, and radius parameters.
